sentences.text: The holotype maxillae contain 13 teeth, whereas a referred specimen preserves 15 teeth.
The holotype skeleton is incomplete but articulated, comprising most of the skull, neck and trunk vertebrae, gastralia, ribs, both humeri, the pelvis, and the majority of the right leg.
Digital reconstruction estimates the skull length at up to 90 centimeters.
The femur measures 95 centimeters in length.
The snout occupies more than 60% of the total skull length and retains a relatively uniform height from front to rear.
The dentary of the holotype bears 16 teeth, a count that falls within the 15-to-18 range seen in Gorgosaurus.
The generic name combines Greek words meaning "terrible" or "frightening" and "lizard".
The specific epithet derives from Latin terms for "solitary" and "mountain".
Stuart Plotkin uncovered the holotype skeleton in 2010 within the upper Oldman Formation of Alberta, Canada.
Two isolated maxillae from unknown localities were tentatively assigned to the species, representing a mature individual and a small juvenile.
Plotkin also reported tyrannosaurid remains from the upper zone of the Oldman Formation near the Provincial Dinosaur Park in 2010.
A University of Alberta team assisted with the excavation between 2010 and 2011.
The holotype is catalogued as UALVP 52981 and is stored at the University of Alberta's Vertebrate Paleontology Laboratory.
Specimens TMP 1994.012.0602 and TMP 1995.005.0001 were referred to the species based on shared anatomical traits with the holotype.
Additional isolated maxillae, UALVP 56605 from a mature individual and TMP 1985.011.0003 from a juvenile, were tentatively linked to Tromerosaurus.
Tromerosaurus is placed within the subfamily Albertosaurinae, though it exhibits some features typical of tyrannosaurines.
Parsimony analyses recover it as the most basal member of Albertosaurinae, a group that also includes Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus.
Bayesian analysis by Powers et al. (2026) instead positions Tromerosaurus as the most basal tyrannosaurine, sister to Albertosaurinae.
Tromerosaurus lived during the Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Canada.
Bayesian results conflict with parsimony findings, highlighting a mosaic anatomy that combines traits of both albertosaurines and early tyrannosaurines.
